name: Battle of Thermopylae
info: In 480 BCE a Greek force led by the Spartan king Leonidas I held the pass of Thermopylae for several days against the Persian army of Xerxes, until the Persians found a path behind them and killed the Greek rearguard.

facts.date: 480 BCE, between July and September; the Persian army was sighted in mid-August, and the fighting lasted three days
facts.place: The pass of Thermopylae, on the Malian Gulf, in central Greece; the pass is now several kilometres inland because of sedimentation
facts.sides: An alliance of Greek city-states led by Sparta under King Leonidas I, about 7,000 men by the usual modern reckoning, of whom an estimated 300 were Spartans; the Achaemenid Persian Empire under Xerxes, with modern estimates of the whole army generally between 120,000 and 300,000, where Herodotus gives 2.6 million
facts.outcome: The Persians forced the pass after a mountain path was revealed to them, and the Greek rearguard was killed, apart from the Thebans, most of whom reportedly surrendered. The Persians went on to overrun Boeotia and take Athens.

t: Ancient and modern figures for the Persian army are far apart: Herodotus gives 2.6 million military personnel, Ctesias 800,000, and modern scholars generally 120,000 to 300,000.
The Persians attacked the Greek position frontally on two days without success, and passed it only when a local man, Ephialtes, told Xerxes of the mountain path.
Thermopylae was a defeat for the Greeks in the war, but the stand of the rearguard became one of the most remembered episodes of the Greco-Persian Wars.
dyk: A hill on which the Greeks were thought to have died was identified differently after 1939, when the archaeologist Spyridon Marinatos found large numbers of Persian bronze arrowheads on Kolonos Hill.
ev: A Persian expedition destroys Eretria but is met at Marathon by a heavily outnumbered Athenian army, and the Persians withdraw to Asia
A congress at Corinth forms a confederate alliance of Greek city-states
The Greeks leave the Vale of Tempe and adopt Themistocles's plan to hold Thermopylae on land and the straits of Artemisium at sea
The Persian army is sighted across the Malian Gulf, and Leonidas refuses Xerxes's demand that the Greeks hand over their arms
Persian assaults on the first two days fail, and Ephialtes tells Xerxes of the mountain path
On the third day the Greek rearguard is surrounded and killed and the pass is opened
The Greek fleet defeats the Persian fleet at the Battle of Salamis
A Greek army defeats Mardonius at the Battle of Plataea, ending the invasion

sections.background:
Athens and Eretria had aided the Ionian Revolt against the Persian Empire of Darius I in 499–494 BCE, and Darius vowed to punish those involved, especially the Athenians. In 491 BCE he asked the Greek city-states for earth and water as tokens of submission. Most gave them, but in Athens the ambassadors were put on trial and thrown into a pit, and in Sparta they were thrown down a well. The expedition of 490 BCE under Datis and Artaphernes destroyed Eretria, but at Marathon it met a heavily outnumbered Athenian army and the Persians withdrew to Asia.

Darius began raising a new army, but his Egyptian province revolted in 486 BCE, and he died while preparing to march on Egypt. His son Xerxes crushed the revolt and prepared a full-scale invasion with stockpiling and conscription, bridging the Hellespont and having a canal dug across the isthmus of Mount Athos. In early 480 BCE the army mustered at Sardis crossed the Hellespont on two pontoon bridges, and many Greek cities gave earth and water.

Athens had been building a large fleet of triremes since 482 BCE under Themistocles. Xerxes deliberately left Athens and Sparta out of his demand, and support gathered around them. A congress at Corinth in late autumn 481 BCE formed an alliance of Greek city-states. A force of 10,000 hoplites sent to the Vale of Tempe withdrew after Alexander I of Macedon warned that the vale could be bypassed. Themistocles then proposed holding the pass of Thermopylae while the allied navies blocked the straits of Artemisium.
sections.forces:
The Persian numbers have been disputed at length. Herodotus claimed 2.6 million military personnel, with as many support personnel; the contemporary poet Simonides speaks of four million, and Ctesias gave 800,000 as the total assembled. Modern scholars tend to reject these figures as miscalculations or exaggerations by the victors and generally estimate 120,000 to 300,000. The numbers at Thermopylae are as uncertain, since it is unclear whether the whole army marched there or Xerxes left garrisons in Macedon and Thessaly.

Leonidas I, one of the Spartan kings, marched ahead of the main Spartan army, which was held back by the festival of Carneia and the Olympic truce. He took the 300 men of the royal bodyguard, the Hippeis; Herodotus says he chose only men with living sons. Contingents joined on the way, and the force numbered more than 7,000 at the pass. The sources differ on its makeup: Diodorus gives 1,000 Lacedemonians and 3,000 other Peloponnesians, while Herodotus tallies 3,100 Peloponnesians in one passage and gives 4,000 in another. Many modern historians add 1,000 Lacedemonians and 900 helots to Herodotus's 5,200 for about 7,000, though other combinations are plausible.

Leonidas camped at the middle gate, the narrowest part of the pass, where the Phocians had built a wall. A hoplite phalanx could block it with no risk of being outflanked by cavalry. The weak point was a mountain track across the highland, which people from Trachis told Leonidas of, and he stationed 1,000 Phocians on the heights.
sections.course:
The Persian army was sighted across the Malian Gulf in mid-August. Xerxes sent an emissary offering freedom, the title "Friends of the Persian People" and better land. Leonidas refused, and to the written demand to hand over arms he is reported to have answered "Molṑn labé", usually translated "come and take them". Xerxes waited four days for the Greeks to disperse. On the first day of battle he ordered 5,000 archers to shoot, to little effect, then sent 10,000 Medes and Cissians in frontal assaults. The Greeks fought before the Phocian wall, each city's unit kept together and rotated. According to Ctesias the first wave was "cut to ribbons", with only two or three Spartans killed. Herodotus and Diodorus say Xerxes then sent the Immortals, 10,000 men, who fared no better.

The second day went no better. Later that day Ephialtes, a Trachinian seeking a reward, told Xerxes of the path. Herodotus reports that he sent Hydarnes with the Immortals that evening; Diodorus gives Hydarnes 20,000 men. At daybreak on the third day the Phocians on the path noticed the column by the rustling of oak leaves, withdrew to a hill, and were bypassed after a volley of arrows.

Leonidas called a council of war at dawn. Many Greeks left, and around 2,000 stayed. The 700 Thespians under Demophilus refused to go, and the 400 Thebans and probably the helots also remained. Herodotus admits doubt whether the others withdrew without orders or at Leonidas's command. The Greeks advanced into the wider part of the pass and fought with spears until they broke, then with short swords. Leonidas was shot down by archers and the two sides fought over his body. The rest withdrew to a hill behind the wall, the Thebans surrendered, and the others were shot down with arrows.
sections.aftermath:
According to Herodotus the pass was opened to the Persians at a cost of up to 20,000 dead. The Greek rearguard was annihilated, with a probable loss of 2,000 including the dead of the first two days. Herodotus at one point says 4,000 Greeks died, a figure that is probably too high. The king later had the Theban prisoners branded with the royal mark. The Greeks buried their dead on the hill, and forty years after the battle Leonidas's bones were returned to Sparta and buried with full honours, with funeral games held in his memory every year.

The simultaneous naval battle at Artemisium had been a tactical stalemate, and with the pass lost the Greek fleet retreated to the Saronic Gulf, where it helped ferry the remaining Athenians to Salamis. The Persian army sacked and burned Plataea and Thespiae and took the evacuated city of Athens. The Peloponnesians demolished the road across the Isthmus of Corinth and built a wall. Themistocles persuaded the Greeks to seek a decisive victory against the Persian fleet, and at Salamis in late 480 BCE they destroyed much of it.

Xerxes withdrew with much of his army to Asia, reportedly losing many of his troops to starvation and disease, and left Mardonius to continue the campaign. The next year a Greek army defeated Mardonius at the Battle of Plataea, ending the invasion, and the Greeks destroyed much of the remaining Persian fleet at Mycale.
sections.sources:
The principal ancient account is Herodotus, supplemented by Diodorus Siculus, Pausanias and Plutarch, with Ctesias's figures for the first wave and the whole army. The poet Simonides, a contemporary, wrote epigrams commemorating the dead, the earliest known appearance of the battle in culture. The accounts disagree on numbers, as set out above, and modern historians, who usually consider Herodotus more reliable, build their figures on his. Herodotus himself admits doubt about whether most of the Greek contingents left on Leonidas's order. Herodotus also reports a consultation of the Oracle at Delphi, and the anecdotes about Leonidas and the Spartans, such as his exchange with his wife Gorgo, are described as apocryphal and not verifiable.

Historians also dispute the Thebans. Herodotus suggests they were hostages to ensure Thebes's good behaviour; Plutarch argued that hostages would have been sent away with the rest, and the likelier explanation is that they were Theban loyalists who objected to Persian domination. Archaeology bears on the site. The pass is often said to have been so narrow that only one chariot could pass, but recent core samples indicate it was about 100 metres wide, with the sea reaching the gates. In 1939 Marinatos found Persian arrowheads on Kolonos Hill, which changed the identification of the hill of the last stand.

Why Leonidas stayed is also debated. It is said that he obeyed Spartan law, that he acted on the Oracle's words, or, in a commonly accepted theory, that he formed a rearguard so that the others could get away, which could save more than 3,000 men.
sections.legacy:
Within the Persian invasion Thermopylae was undoubtedly a defeat for the Greeks and forcing the pass a strategic Persian victory, though the retreat of most of the Greek troops was in its way a victory too. The battle showed that the Greeks could fight effectively against the Persians, and the defeat made Leonidas and his men martyrs, which raised Greek morale. It is disputed that the stand bought much time before Salamis: about one month passed, and George Cawkwell suggests Xerxes's own delay in reducing Phocis and Boeotia explains the gap. Cawkwell speaks of a "brilliant success" for Xerxes, and Lazenby calls the Greek defeat "disastrous".

The fame of the battle rests chiefly on the example it set. Contemporary Greeks saw in it a contrast between a small free people and imperial subjects, a view that can be seen as a sweeping overgeneralisation. A well-known epigram, usually attributed to Simonides, was engraved on a stone above the burial mound of the Spartans: "O stranger, tell the Lacedaemonians that we lie here, obedient to their words". The original stone has not survived; a new one was engraved in 1955. The site has a Leonidas Monument by Vassos Falireas, with the words "Molṑn labé", and a monument to the 700 Thespians, unveiled in 1997.

Interest in the battle in Europe revived in the 1700s with the poems Leonidas by Richard Glover (1737) and by Willem van Haren (1742). Steven Pressfield's novel Gates of Fire (1998) is unusual in depicting the battle as gruesome. Zack Snyder's film 300 (2006), based on Frank Miller's comic series, grossed US$456 million globally. The Battle of the Persian Gate in 330 BCE has been called "the Persian Thermopylae".

summary: At Thermopylae in 480 BCE a Greek force under the Spartan king Leonidas I blocked the pass against the army of Xerxes for several days, until Persian troops reached their rear by a mountain path and the Greek rearguard was killed. It was a Persian victory in the campaign, and the stand became widely remembered.
references: Paul Cartledge, Thermopylae: The Battle That Changed the World (Pan, 2007)
Ernle Bradford, Thermopylae: the battle for the West (Da Capo Press, 2004)
notes: Date: the article says 480 BCE, 'between July and September', and gives both 'late August or early September' (arrival at the pass) and 'mid-August' (Persian army sighted); these sit uneasily together. I gave 'between July and September' as the span and used mid-August only for the sighting, as the article words it.
Persian estimates: the article names 'Robert von fischer' (40,000) and 'Hans' (65,000) with no surnames or detail; reproduced as given, and the passage is garbled in the article.

Greek numbers: the table of contingents is missing from the saved article; I gave only the figures in the prose (7,000, 3,100, 4,000, 5,200, 1,000 Lacedemonians, 900 helots, Pausanias's 6,000 Locrians left out).

Greek dead: the article says a 'probable loss of 2,000' and that Herodotus's 4,000 is probably too high; I gave both. Persian dead 'up to 20,000' is given as Herodotus's, as the article attributes it.
The article says 'around 2,000 soldiers stayed' but its other passages say 300 Spartans, 700 Thespians, 400 Thebans and possibly 900 helots; not reconciled.

The article says the pass was 'ideally suited' and the Greek position 'nearly impregnable'; I left these evaluative lines out. The article also contains praise quotations and a 'free men against slaves' passage, of which I kept only a neutral mention.

Left out: Leonidas's other replies, Demaratus and the scout, Tigranes's remark, the Oracle's verse text, the prophecy, Gorgo's answer (named as an anecdote only), Diodorus's Tyrrhastiadas, the Gaulish attack of later date, 1941 defence, the coins.
Marinatos's find is described as changing the identification of the hill; the dyk wording follows the article.
